title: Revisiting Graph Adversarial Attack: A Perspective of Budget Optimization

problem.claim: Graph adversarial attacks seek to cause graph-based machine learning models to produce incorrect predictions through carefully designed perturbations.

gap.claim: Existing graph adversarial attack strategies can produce ineffective and redundant perturbations that consume attack budget and increase detection likelihood.

contributions.claim: The paper proposes Budget-Reduced Attack Filtering (BRAF) frameworks to eliminate ineffective perturbations produced by existing graph adversarial attack methods and optimize the attack budget.
The paper provides code for the proposed work.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments validate the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed filtering frameworks.

narrative_sequence.summary: Graph adversarial attacks target graph-structured data and manipulate graph elements to affect model predictions.
These attacks exploit model vulnerabilities by maximizing performance degradation with minimal perturbations.
Incomplete attack strategies can generate redundant ineffective perturbations that waste budget and increase detection risk.
The paper proposes BRAF frameworks to filter ineffective perturbations and optimize attack budgets.
The authors report extensive experimental validation of effectiveness and scalability and provide code.

source_observation.claim: Ineffective perturbations can consume an adversarial attack budget and increase detection likelihood.

interpretation.claim: Filtering ineffective actions may improve the efficiency and stealth of budget-constrained attack strategies.

application.claim: For graph attack systems, evaluate whether proposed perturbations contribute meaningfully before spending additional attack budget.

exception.claim: The abstract does not specify when a perturbation is classified as ineffective or how filtering affects individual attack settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the BRAF framework algorithms or filtering criteria.
The abstract does not report datasets, baselines, quantitative results, or experimental conditions.
The abstract does not establish independent verification of the reported effectiveness or scalability.
